problem:
Title: Inequality of Hölder Means

Let $p, q \in \overline \R$ be [[Definition:Extended Real Number Line|extended real numbers]] such that $p < q$.

Let $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n \ge 0$ be [[Definition:Real Number|real numbers]].

If $p < 0$, then we require that $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n > 0$.

Then the [[Definition:Hölder Mean|Hölder mean]] satisfies the inequality:
:$\map {M_p} {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} \le \map {M_q} {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$

Equality holds {{iff}}:
:$x_1 = x_2 = \cdots = x_n$
or:
:$q < 0$ and $x_k = 0$ for at least one $k \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n}$.

Note that in particular:
:$\forall p \in \R: \map {M_{-\infty} } {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} \le \map {M_p} {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$

and:
:$\forall p \in \R: \map {M_\infty} {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} \ge \map {M_p} {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$
proof_numbered:
0001 | For [[Definition:Real Number|real]] $p \ne 0$, the [[Definition:Hölder Mean|Hölder mean]] is defined as:
0002 | :$\ds \map {M_p} {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} = \paren {\frac 1 n \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n {x_k}^p}^{1 / p}$
0003 | whenever the above expression is defined.
0004 | 
0005 | First we note that by definition of [[Definition:Hölder Mean with Positive Infinite Exponent|Hölder mean with $p = \infty$]]:
0006 | :$\map {M_\infty} {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} = \max \set {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$
0007 | 
0008 | This is justified by [[Limit of Hölder Mean as Exponent tends to Infinity]]:
0009 | :$\ds \lim_{p \mathop \to +\infty} \map {M_p} {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} = \max \set {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$
0010 | 
0011 | From [[Maximum is Greater than or Equal to Hölder Mean]]:
0012 | :$\max \set {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} \ge \map {M_p} {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$
0013 | 
0014 | and so:
0015 | :$\forall p \in \R: \map {M_\infty} {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} \ge \map {M_p} {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$
0016 | {{qed|lemma}}
0017 | 
0018 | Similarly, by definition of [[Definition:Hölder Mean with Negative Infinite Exponent|Hölder mean with $p = -\infty$]]:
0019 | :$\map {M_{-\infty} } {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} = \min \set {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$
0020 | 
0021 | This is justified by [[Limit of Hölder Mean as Exponent tends to Negative Infinity]]:
0022 | :$\ds \lim_{p \mathop \to -\infty} \map {M_p} {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} = \min \set {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$
0023 | 
0024 | From [[Minimum is Less than or Equal to Hölder Mean]]:
0025 | :$\min \set {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} \le \map {M_p} {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$
0026 | 
0027 | and so:
0028 | :$\forall p \in \R: \map {M_{-\infty} } {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} \le \map {M_p} {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$
0029 | {{qed|lemma}}
0030 | 
0031 | Let either $p = 0$ or $q = 0$.
0032 | 
0033 | By definition of [[Definition:Hölder Mean with Zero Exponent|Hölder mean with $p = 0$]]:
0034 | :$\map {M_0} {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} = \map G {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$
0035 | where $G$ denotes the [[Definition:Geometric Mean|geometric mean]].
0036 | 
0037 | This is justified by [[Limit of Hölder Mean as Exponent tends to Zero is Geometric Mean]]:
0038 | :$\ds \lim_{p \mathop \to 0} \map {M_p} {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} = \map G {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$
0039 | 
0040 | It remains to resolve the inequality for $p, q \in \R_{\ge 0}$.
0041 | 
0042 | Consider the [[Definition:Real Function|function]] $\phi: \R_{\ge 0} \to \R_{\ge 0}$ defined as:
0043 | :$\forall x \in \R_{\ge 0}: \map \phi x = x^{q/p}$
0044 | 
0045 | By the [[Power Rule for Derivatives]]:
0046 | :$\map {D_x} {x^{q / p} } = \dfrac q p x^{q / p - 1}$
0047 | 
0048 | From [[Real Function is Strictly Convex iff Derivative is Strictly Increasing]]:
0049 | :$\phi$ is [[Definition:Strictly Convex Real Function|strictly convex]] if $q > 0$.
0050 | 
0051 | From [[Real Function is Strictly Concave iff Derivative is Strictly Decreasing]]:
0052 | :$\phi$ is [[Definition:Strictly Concave Real Function|strictly concave]] if $q < 0$.
0053 | 
0054 | Now apply [[Jensen's Inequality (Real Analysis)|Jensen's inequality]] to ${x_1}^p, {x_2}^p, \ldots, {x_n}^p$.
0055 | 
0056 | For $q > 0$, this gives:
0057 | :$\ds \paren {\frac 1 n \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n {x_k}^p}^{q/p} \le \frac 1 n \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n {x_k}^q$
0058 | 
0059 | For $q < 0$, the reverse inequality holds.
0060 | 
0061 | Also by [[Jensen's Inequality (Real Analysis)|Jensen's inequality]], equality holds {{iff}} $x_1 = x_2 = \cdots = x_n$.
0062 | 
0063 | In either case, the result follows.
0064 | {{qed}}
